description: Egbere are malevolent nocturnal goblins in Yoruba (not Igbo) folklore. Short-statured forest/grave dwellers who emerge at midnight weeping and riding sheep. They guard a mat of wealth; seizing it grants riches, though their tears are feigned. Documented by Crowther (1852) and Taylor (1898) in Yoruba accounts.
source: Crowther & Vidal, 'A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language' (1852); Taylor, 'The Flaming Torch in Darkest Africa' (1898); Yoruba oral tradition
research_notes: Record incorrectly attributes Egbere to Igbo culture; it is Yoruba. Corrected culture attribution in description.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon cosmology centers on Amma, Nommo, and the Pale Fox (Ogo); no panther guardian appears in Griaule's or Dieterlen's ethnographies. The closest analogue is the Kanaga mask's antelope symbolism. Record appears fabricated from generic 'forest guardian' templates.
source: Griaule, 'Conversations With Ogotemmêli' (1965); Dogon ethnographic surveys
research_notes: No panther guardian in Dogon mythology. Record likely conflates generic African forest guardian tropes with Dogon culture.

description: Not independently attested in Yoruba tradition. Yoruba orisha pantheon includes Ogun, Oshun, Yemoja, and Shango, but no specific panther nature-spirit. Leopards appear as royal symbols and in Egungun masquerades, not as distinct nature-spirits. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.
source: Yoruba religion ethnographies (Abimbola, Idowu); no panther nature-spirit documented
research_notes: No panther nature-spirit in Yoruba folklore. Description's claim of 'embodying the ocean' is incoherent for a forest panther.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon spiritual beings are Nommo (amphibious ancestors), Ogo (Pale Fox), and Lebe (serpent ancestor). No panther spirit appears in Griaule's documentation. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.
source: Griaule & Dieterlen Dogon ethnographies; no panther spirit documented
research_notes: No panther spirit in Dogon cosmology. Record's 'lake embodiment' claim contradicts Dogon landlocked geography.

description: Peixe Caball ('horse-fish') is a Cape Verdean mermaid-like being with an equine upper body and fish tail, inhabiting deep ocean and coastal reefs. It appears to sailors as an omen of calm seas and represents the fusion of land and sea in islander identity. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition and folkloric collections.
source: Cape Verdean oral tradition; folkloric collections of Lusophone Atlantic islands
research_notes: Attested in Cape Verdean folklore. The name is Portuguese-based creole ('peixe' = fish, 'caball' = horse).

description: Passadinha is a trickster bird in Cape Verdean folklore, known for vocal mimicry and mischief in village gardens and forests. It embodies wit and playfulness, deceiving humans through imitation. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tales alongside figures like Ti Lobo and Chibinho.
source: Cape Verdean oral tradition; 'Ti Lobo and Chibinho' folk narratives
research_notes: Attested Cape Verdean trickster bird. Name derives from Portuguese 'passarinha' (little bird).

description: Not independently attested in Ghanaian tradition. 'Mixtec' refers to a Mesoamerican people of Oaxaca, Mexico; the record's description details a Chilean pudu deer guardian of Nothofagus forests with volcanoes and lapis lazuli — entirely South American. No deer guardian exists in Ghanaian Akan, Ewe, or Ga folklore.
source: Mixtec/Mesoamerican ethnography (not West African); Chilean Mapuche pudu folklore
research_notes: Complete misattribution: Mixtec is Mexican, description is Chilean. No deer guardian in Ghanaian folklore.

description: In Wolof and broader Senegalese folklore, jinn (djinn) are supernatural beings of smokeless fire, integrated from Islamic tradition into pre-existing spirit beliefs. They shapeshift (often as snakes), inhabit ruins and deserts, and can be mischievous or helpful. Iron and Qur'anic verses repel them. Not merely tricksters — they occupy a parallel moral universe accountable to God.
source: Wolof oral tradition; Islamic syncretism in Senegal (McLaughlin, 'Islam and Popular Worship'); Quran Surah Al-Jinn
research_notes: Attested in Wolof/Senegalese folklore as Islamic-integrated spirits. Record's 'trickster' label oversimplifies their complex theology.

description: Not independently attested in Malian tradition. Coyotes are North/Central American; Maya civilization is Mesoamerican. The record's description of a Maya forest spirit overseeing a maize covenant with Yum Kaax is authentically Yucatec Maya but entirely misplaced in Mali. No coyote spirits exist in Dogon, Bambara, or Mandinka cosmologies.
source: Maya religion (Thompson, 'Maya History and Religion'); not West African
research_notes: Complete geographic/cultural mismatch: Maya/Mesoamerican entity misattributed to Mali.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct named entity in Yoruba tradition. Cranes (grey crowned cranes) appear in Yoruba iconography as symbols of longevity and in Ogboni regalia, but no specific 'Crane Ghost' haunting swamps as an ancestor messenger is documented. The record appears to elaborate generic water-spirit tropes with crane imagery.
source: Yoruba religion ethnographies (Idowu, Abimbola); no 'Crane Ghost' documented
research_notes: No distinct 'Crane Ghost' in Yoruba folklore. Cranes are symbolic, not ghostly entities.

description: Capotona is a mournful coastal ghost in Cape Verdean folklore, haunting shorelines and abandoned lighthouses. It manifests as a spectral figure emitting mournful sounds, countered by sunrise. Represents the perils of the sea and lost sailors. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition alongside Catchorrona.
source: Cape Verdean oral tradition; 'Lady Barbro of Brokind' and 'Ti Lobo and Chibinho' story collections
research_notes: Attested Cape Verdean coastal ghost. Name likely from Portuguese 'cabo' (cape) + 'tona' (tone/sound).

description: Catchorrona ('black dog') is an ominous spectral hound in Cape Verdean folklore, appearing at moonlit crossroads to warn or terrify night wanderers. It induces fear and stealth, repelled by silver bells. Represents dangers of nocturnal travel. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition.
source: Cape Verdean oral tradition; 'Lady Barbro of Brokind' and 'Ti Lobo and Chibinho' story collections
research_notes: Attested Cape Verdean spectral black dog. Parallels European 'Black Shuck' but in creole island context.

description: Vodun is the Fon/Ewe/Aja religion of Benin/Togo/Ghana venerating hundreds of spirits (vodún) under Nana Buluku and Mawu-Lisa. Key spirits: Legba (crossroads), Sakpata (earth/smallpox), Xêbioso (thunder), Gû (iron/war), Dàn (serpent wealth), Mami Wata (water wealth). Living priesthood tradition; Benin's national religion since 1990s.
source: Rosenthal, 'Possession, Ecstasy, and Law in Ewe Voodoo' (1998); Landry, 'Vodún' (2019); Blier, 'African Vodun' (1995); Benin ethnographic record
research_notes: Record treats 'Vodun Spirits' as a single creature; corrected to describe the Vodun pantheon system accurately.

description: Obayifo is an Ashanti (Akan, Ghana) vampire-witch who appears human by day but at night emits phosphorescent light from armpits and anus, flies as a ball of light, and sucks blood/vitality. Known as asiman in Dahomey. Associated with witchcraft (bayi), infant mortality, and food obsession. No defense exists. Documented in Rattray's Ashanti ethnography.
source: Rattray, 'Ashanti' (1923); Bunson, 'The Vampire Encyclopedia' (1993); Akan oral tradition
research_notes: Attested Ashanti vampire-witch. Record's 'ogre' type incorrect; it is a witch/vampire entity.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct named entity in Wolof tradition. Wolof water spirits (jinés/jinn) inhabit rivers and coasts but no specific 'octopus water-spirit' appears in ethnographic records (Diop, Faye). The octopus motif may reflect Atlantic marine influence but lacks attestation.
source: Wolof ethnography (Diop, 'L'Islam et les sociétés wolof'); no octopus spirit documented
research_notes: No octopus water-spirit in Wolof folklore. Record appears to invent a specific zoomorphic water spirit.

description: Ogbanje (Ọgbanje) are Igbo 'spirit children' who cyclically die and are reborn into the same family, causing recurrent grief. They possess a hidden iyi-uwa stone linking them to the spirit world; destroying it ends the cycle. Linked to sickle-cell disease and SIDS in medical anthropology. Documented in Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart' and Igbo ethnography.
source: Achebe, 'Things Fall Apart' (1958); Nzewi, 'Malevolent ọgbanje' (2001); Igbo oral tradition (Odinani)
research_notes: Well-attested Igbo spirit child phenomenon. Record's 'forest spirit' type incorrect; it is a familial reincarnation spirit.

description: Ogun (Ògún) is a primordial Yoruba orisha of iron, war, blacksmithing, hunting, and technology. He cleared the path for other orisha to enter Earth with a machete and dog. Patron of warriors, smiths, drivers; oaths sworn on iron invoke him. Venerated across Yoruba, Dahomey, Vodun, Candomblé, Santería. Not a water spirit — his element is earth/iron.
source: Barnes, 'Africa's Ogun' (1997); Idowu, 'Olodumare' (1962); Yoruba oral tradition (oríkì)
research_notes: Record incorrectly classifies Ogun as 'water-spirit'; corrected to iron/war orisha. Major deity, not minor spirit.

description: Olokun is the Yoruba orisha of the deep ocean, owner of the sea, parent of Ajé (wealth). Androgynous: male in coastal areas, female inland. Grants prosperity to fishermen/traders; withdraws wealth when disrespected. Keeper of subconscious secrets. Imprisoned by Obatala with Ogun's chain after flooding land. Venerated in Lagos festivals and diaspora.
source: Murphy, 'Ọ̀ṣun across the Waters' (2001); Clark, 'Santería' (2007); Yoruba oral tradition
research_notes: Attested major Yoruba orisha. Record's 'water-spirit' archetype is correct but understates divine status.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon ancestor spirits are the Nommo (amphibious) and Lebe (serpent). Owls appear in Dogon iconography on sanctuary doors but not as named ancestor-spirits guarding valleys. Record appears fabricated from generic 'owl guardian' templates.
source: Griaule & Dieterlen Dogon ethnographies; no owl ancestor-spirit documented
research_notes: No owl ancestor-spirit in Dogon cosmology. Record's 'valley guardian' role is generic.

description: Not independently attested in Ashanti (Akan) tradition. Owls in Akan folklore are often witch familiars or omens (e.g., 'koko' owl), not benevolent nature-spirits guarding valleys. No named 'Owl Nature-Spirit' appears in Rattray or Ashanti ethnographies. Record appears fabricated.
source: Rattray, 'Ashanti' (1923); Akan folklore collections; no owl nature-spirit documented
research_notes: No owl nature-spirit in Ashanti tradition. Owls are typically ominous, not guardians.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon water spirits are the Nommo (amphibious ancestors). No owl water-spirit appears in Griaule's documentation of Dogon cosmogony. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.
source: Griaule, 'Conversations With Ogotemmêli' (1965); no owl water-spirit documented
research_notes: No owl water-spirit in Dogon cosmology. Nommo are the sole water spirits.

description: Ogo (Yurugu), the Pale Fox, is the Dogon trickster. Firstborn of Amma, he rebelled, stole a piece of the sun, and brought death, imperfection, and speech to humanity. His incest with Earth produced first ancestors. Amma restored order by sacrificing his twin Nommo. Ogo's disorder is necessary for a dynamic universe. Per Griaule's Ogotemmêli interviews.
source: Griaule, 'Conversations With Ogotemmêli' (1965); Dogon oral tradition (Ogotemmêli narratives)
research_notes: Attested Dogon cosmic trickster (Pale Fox). Record's 'shadow' element and 'Void' habitat are poetic elaborations; core myth is accurate.

description: Zin are Hausa water spirits inhabiting the Niger River and lakes in Niger and northern Nigeria. They shapeshift between aquatic and human forms, luring humans to watery domains. Feared as causes of drowning and disappearances. Related to broader West African water spirit complexes (Mami Wata, Ndi Mmili). Documented in Hausa oral tradition.
source: Hausa oral tradition; 'Bori' spirit possession ethnography (Tremearne, 'Hausa Superstitions'); Niger River folklore
research_notes: Attested Hausa water spirits. Record's 'Niger' country correct; culture should be Hausa not generic 'Niger'.

description: Ndi Mmili ('people of the water') are powerful Igbo water spirits dwelling in rivers and lakes. They embody life, fertility, beauty, and wealth; invoked for blessings during hardship. Female-centered cult; priestesses mediate. Distinct from Mami Wata though syncretized. Documented in Igbo cosmology and ethnography.
source: Igbo oral tradition (Odinani); Nwoga, 'Igbo Traditional Religion'; ethnographic surveys of southeastern Nigeria
research_notes: Attested Igbo water spirits. Record's 'Nigeria' country correct; culture should be Igbo not generic 'Nigeria'.

description: Nimba (D'mba) is the Baga (Guinea) great mother headdress spirit, a monumental carved wooden bust worn in harvest dances. She embodies fertility, abundance, and the ideal woman — not a forest guardian. Appears as an elderly woman testing visitors' respect in some narratives. Documented in Baga art and ritual (Smithsonian, Musée du Quai Branly collections).
source: Baga oral tradition; Arnoldi, 'Bamana Sculpture' (1986); Museum collections (Met, Smithsonian, Quai Branly)
research_notes: Record misidentifies Nimba as generic 'forest guardian'; it is specifically Baga mother/fertility headdress spirit.

description: Ninki Nanka is the Mandinka (Gambia/Senegal) dragon-like water spirit: a 30-foot reptilian creature with crocodile head, donkey/hippopotamus-giraffe body, mirror scales, and fatal Medusa-like stare. Inhabits swamps and caves; explains river disappearances. Carries a head gem of power. Documented in Mandinka oral tradition and 1906 colonial reports; investigated by CFZ expedition 2006.
source: Mandinka oral tradition; Sarr, 'Islam, Power, and Dependency in the Gambia River Basin' (2016); CFZ Gambia Expedition (2006); BBC report
research_notes: Attested Mandinka dragon. Record's 'Gambia' country correct; culture should be Mandinka not generic 'Gambia'.

description: Nommo (Nummo) are Dogon primordial amphibious ancestral spirits, created by Amma as first living beings. Hermaphroditic, fish-tailed humanoids who descended from Sirius in an ark of fire and thunder, created water reservoirs, and sacrificed their bodies to populate the universe with Binu shrines. Masters of Water, Teachers, Monitors. Central to Dogon cosmogony per Griaule's Ogotemmêli interviews.
source: Griaule, 'Conversations With Ogotemmêli' (1965); Dieterlen; Dogon oral tradition (Ogotemmêli)
research_notes: Attested Dogon primordial ancestors. Record's 'water-spirit' type correct but understates cosmic role.

description: Not independently attested as a West African creature. Ntsomi is Xhosa (South Africa) women's solo performance art combining storytelling, dance, and song with props — not a monster or forest spirit. Documented by Harold Scheub ('The Xhosa Ntsomi'). The record misattributes a South African performance tradition to West Africa as a creature.
source: Scheub, 'The Xhosa Ntsomi' (1975); Xhosa oral performance tradition (South Africa)
research_notes: Complete misattribution: Ntsomi is Xhosa performance art from South Africa, not a West African creature.

description: Nyerum are Bambara (Mali) water spirits inhabiting seasonal floodplains and ponds. They breathe water, immune to drought, and lure/drown intruders. Part of Bambara animistic tradition alongside Faro (river spirit) and pond genies. Documented in Bambara oral tradition and ethnographic surveys of Niger River communities.
source: Bambara oral tradition; Imperato, 'Bambara' ethnography; West African water spirit comparative studies
research_notes: Attested Bambara water spirits. Record's 'Mali' country correct; culture should be Bambara not generic 'Mali'.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon are landlocked in Mali's Bandiagara cliffs; whales do not feature in their cosmology. Ancestor spirits are Nommo (amphibious) and Lebe (serpent). The 'whale ancestor-spirit guarding undergrounds' appears fabricated, possibly conflating Nommo's fish-tail with whale imagery.
source: Griaule & Dieterlen Dogon ethnographies; no whale spirits documented
research_notes: No whale spirits in landlocked Dogon culture. Fabricated from Nommo fish-tail misinterpretation.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon animal spirits include the Pale Fox (Ogo), Jackal, and various mask animals (antelope, hyena, monkey); no whale. The 'whale animal-spirit guarding valleys' is fabricated, likely from same Nommo conflation as the ancestor-spirit variant.
source: Griaule & Dieterlen Dogon ethnographies; no whale animal-spirit documented
research_notes: No whale animal-spirit in Dogon culture. Duplicate fabrication with ancestor-spirit variant.

description: Not independently attested in Yoruba tradition. Yoruba water spirits include Olokun (ocean), Yemoja (rivers), Oshun (freshwater); no whale ghost guarding hills. Whales occasionally beach in Nigeria but lack mythological personification. Record appears fabricated from generic 'whale ghost' templates.
source: Yoruba religion ethnographies (Idowu, Abimbola); no whale ghost documented
research_notes: No whale ghost in Yoruba folklore. Hills habitat contradicts whale ecology.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon trickster is exclusively Ogo (Pale Fox). No whale trickster exists in landlocked Mali. The 'whale trickster guarding rivers' with flight and storm-calling is fabricated, possibly conflating Ogo's chaos with Nommo's water association.
source: Griaule, 'Conversations With Ogotemmêli' (1965); no whale trickster documented
research_notes: No whale trickster in Dogon cosmology. Ogo is the sole trickster.

description: Not independently attested in Nigerian tradition. 'Cheyenne' refers to a Native American Plains people (Montana/Oklahoma); wildcat spirits in Cheyenne tradition relate to cave-dwelling guardians. No Cheyenne wildcat spirit exists in Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, or any Nigerian folklore. Record is a complete cross-continental misattribution.
source: Cheyenne ethnography (Grinnell, 'The Cheyenne Indians'); not Nigerian
research_notes: Complete misattribution: Cheyenne is Native American (USA), not Nigerian. Cave embodiment mismatched.

description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon cliff-dwelling culture features mask animals (walu antelope, satimbe woman, kanaga cross) but no named wildcat spirit guarding cliffs. The record's 'central spirit in Dogon mythology' claim is unsupported by Griaule or Dieterlen. Appears fabricated.
source: Griaule & Dieterlen Dogon ethnographies; no wildcat spirit documented
research_notes: No wildcat spirit in Dogon cosmology. Fabricated guardian role.
